prepared_template.title: Progressive weakness despite treatment for meningitis
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her mid-20s presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of headache and cervical pain accompanied by paraesthesia in the right upper extremity, followed by 2 days of progressive right-sided weakness. She reported difficulty performing fine motor tasks and intermittent febrile episodes. Examination showed right-sided hemiparesis (3/5 right upper extremity, 4/5 right lower extremity), brisk deep tendon reflexes with right upper-extremity hyperreflexia, and reduced cervical spine range of motion.

Relevant history: no significant medical history; vaginal delivery under epidural anaesthesia 3 months earlier; COVID-19 infection 1 month before presentation; no history of spinal surgery or significant spinal trauma.

Initial investigations: non-contrast CT of the head revealed no acute intracranial pathology. Lumbar puncture demonstrated pleocytosis, elevated protein (193 mg/dL) and neutrophil predominance (71.3%). Serological testing for HIV, viral hepatitis and other infectious agents was negative.

She was admitted with a preliminary (working) diagnosis of non-specific bacterial meningitis. Blood and urine cultures were obtained, and empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and ampicillin were started. This diagnosis remained provisional at the decision point.

Despite treatment, her condition deteriorated over the following 3 days: progression to asymmetric tetraparesis with superficial and deep sensory disturbances, urinary dysfunction, a positive Babinski sign, meningeal irritation and anisocoria. C-reactive protein and other inflammatory markers were also elevated.

Recorded limits of the available data at this point: the head CT excluded acute intracranial pathology only; no spinal imaging had been performed. Culture results from blood and urine were pending at the decision point and are not reported here. The remote epidural anaesthesia and recent COVID-19 infection are documented history items; no causal relationship is established in the record.

This is a constructed selected-record review: the findings above were documented at different times (initial presentation, admission, and day 3 of treatment). No pretreatment consolidated time point is implied beyond the recorded sequence. Unreported information is unknown, not normal.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: Answers should recognise the time-critical nature of progressive cord-level signs and propose urgent spinal imaging and escalation; they should not present the pending cultures as already negative, nor treat unreported tests as normal.
